intelligence.essence: Governed Baseline Learning Law: NayaNET may learn workload distributions continuously, but changes to the qualified definition of normal provider behavior require admissible evidence, independently verified scope, preserved incident provenance, regression-sensitive testing, and governed promotion. Unresolved failures may inform investigation but shall not independently establish healthy behavior. No adaptive model may certify its own baseline or weaken a hard safety guarantee. The desired result is a system that can say: 'This provider is handling five times more legitimate traffic, so I updated my workload forecast.' But also: 'This provider's failures have risen gradually. I can predict the deterioration, but I have not accepted it as healthy. The original qualified guarantee remains the standard until independent evidence justifies a change.' That is the difference between a system that merely adapts and a system that learns while preserving truth. The three references, the training-data eligibility states, the promotion gate with its eight obligations, the dual-reference comparison, the settlement watermarks, the race-safe promotion, the B1–B6 fixtures, and the reconstructable receipts are the permanent machinery.
intelligence.falsifier: A candidate promoting itself; unresolved incidents used as positive health evidence; an adaptive forecast replacing the qualified contract; a single aggregate score compensating a failed hard obligation; training data contaminated with unresolved periods; the trainer certifying its own anomaly classifications; a promotion racing a disqualified dataset; a rollback erasing the failed candidate and its receipts; a cold successor unable to reconstruct why a baseline changed.

human_view.meaning: Let the system learn — but never let it learn that broken is normal. Three separate things: the qualified reference (frozen, changed only by governed decision), the adaptive candidate (learning every day in the background, allowed to get smarter, never allowed to declare itself correct), and the promoted baseline (the one actually making decisions, changed only through an evidence gate). Every piece of training data gets a label: verified healthy, verified workload shift, declared maintenance, unresolved anomaly, confirmed regression, insufficient evidence, independently cleared. Only the clean labels can teach the system what 'healthy' means — the unresolved ones can be studied, never used as proof that degraded is fine. Traffic growing fivefold after a real launch? The forecast updates automatically. Failures creeping from 1% to 3% with no good explanation? The model may learn to *predict* it, but it may not *accept* it — the original guarantee stands until independent evidence justifies a change. Promotion runs a gauntlet: legitimate context, training integrity, incident disposition, predictive quality, detection integrity, false-alert control, safety preservation, independent qualification — eight separate gates, no averaging. And every promotion leaves a receipt a future Naya can reconstruct: why it changed, what counted as legitimate, what was excluded, who verified it, what must still be detectable. That's the difference between adapting and learning while preserving truth.

intelligence.learning_lesson: This is the learning-governance layer the calibration stack needed: AER-CAL-2 warns against normalization; AER-CAL-3 builds the machine that cannot normalize. The permanent contributions: the three-reference architecture, the seven-state training-data eligibility, the demand-vs-failure-acceptance separation, the eight-obligation promotion gate with the Promote(B_n) predicate, the dual-reference comparison against slow regressions, the settlement watermarks for late outcomes, the race-safe reversible promotion, the B1–B6 paired fixtures, and the reconstructability standard for learning receipts. Every future adaptive system inherits this: learn continuously, promote only on evidence, never certify yourself.
